This kid is standing in a shoe shop with his feet inside an X-ray machine. And he's staring down at his own wiggling toe bones! This was completely normal.
From the 1920s to the 1950s, lots of shoe shops had one of these. You'd slide your feet into the slot at the bottom, look through the viewer on top, and watch your bones move inside your new shoes.

Kids loved it. They'd beg to go shoe shopping just to see their skeletons. Parents trusted it, because it looked so scientific! But here's the problem. Between your feet and the X-ray tube was a thin sheet of aluminium. About one millimetre thick.

You see, it was like sunbathing your feet in radiation every time you tried on shoes. And the people working there were exposed again and again, all day long. Worst of all? It didn't even help shoes fit better.
In 1957, Pennsylvania became the first state to ban them. By 1960, thirty-four states had. So that magic machine in the shoe shop? It was really just an advertisement that fired X-rays at your feet.
